narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average of accepted students who typically rank near the middle of their class. These low academic standings in law school sent the largest signals that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the next most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 36, your score is only slightly below the average of 37.2 among accepted students, which gave the model some reassurance that you have reasonable aptitude and pulled the prediction modestly toward passing.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.8, also below the accepted average of 3.23, added further concern, though it carried less weight than your law-school performance.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently lower class rankings as the dominant reason to expect difficulty passing the bar, outweighing the modestly encouraging LSAT result.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a bar-preparation course before reapplying. Improving your class rank in future semesters would have the biggest impact on future predictions.
